solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Genial one from Scotland I love on the bottle

parts.note: jo is the Scots word for a sweetheart, someone one loves (as in Burns's 'John Anderson, my jo')
a vial is a small glass bottle

explanation.surface: A cheerful Scot whom the speaker adores is fond of a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the bottle' suggests drinking, but 'on' just joins JO to VIAL. JO is Scottish for sweetheart.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone friendly, good-humoured and warm in manner.

clue.text: Judge stand-up performer of few words (a woman)

indicators.note: in a down clue, standing up means the words are read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a mime artist performs without speaking at all

explanation.surface: A judge assesses a stand-up comedian who hardly speaks, apparently a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stand-up' looks like comedy but is the reversal indicator: A MIME read upwards gives EMIMA, after J.
explanation.definitionFit: Jemima is a female given name, so it names a particular woman.

clue.text: That is one health-food shop caught in check

indicators.note: the pieces are caught inside the word for check, so 'in' signals a container

parts.note: to vet is to check or examine
I is the Roman numeral one
a deli (delicatessen) is a shop selling fine foods
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: That is to say, a health-food store was caught and held in check.
explanation.walkthrough: 'check' looks like part of the story but supplies the container; 'That is' is the plain English for the Latin word.
explanation.definitionFit: Videlicet is the Latin word, abbreviated viz., meaning namely, used to introduce an example.

clue.text: Medicinal plant brewing hall's added to ale ingredients

indicators.note: brewing stirs the ingredients together, so the letters are mixed into a new order

parts.note: the possessive 's adds no letter; just the four letters of hall are used

explanation.surface: A herbal remedy is brewed by adding a hall's worth of ale ingredients.
explanation.walkthrough: HALL and ALE make seven letters which, brewed, give ALLHEAL; 'ingredients' only supports the brewing picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Allheal is a common name for valerian and self-heal, herbs once thought to cure every ailment.

clue.text: All the men on board

parts.note: looks like a ship's full crew, but the 'men' are chess pieces on a board

explanation.surface: Every member of the crew is aboard ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Men' is the usual word for game pieces, and 'board' is the chessboard, not a ship's deck.
explanation.definitionFit: A complete set of chessmen comprises every piece that stands on the board at the start.

clue.text: Grass has very little wait!

parts.note: halfa (or alfa) is esparto grass of North Africa
minute (my-NEWT) means tiny, very little

explanation.surface: The grass owns hardly anything, so pause a moment!
explanation.walkthrough: HALFA is an obscure name for esparto grass; 'has' merely joins it to MINUTE, read as the adjective meaning tiny.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation asks someone to pause briefly before acting, which is what 'wait!' requests.

clue.text: Always the youngster is hugged by mum from Madrid

indicators.note: being hugged means being held inside, so the pieces go within the word for mum

parts.note: 'mum' as in keep quiet, signalled by SH
Peter Pan is the boy who never grows up, forever young

explanation.surface: The child always gets a cuddle from a mother from Madrid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mum' is not a mother but the call for silence; Peter Pan is J. M. Barrie's boy who never grows up.
explanation.definitionFit: Spanish describes things belonging to Spain, whose capital city is Madrid.

clue.text: Sit here? Yes and no

definitions.meaning: a grandstand at a sports ground is where spectators sit
the verb means to be on one's feet, the reverse of sitting, so it both is and is not a place to sit

explanation.surface: Someone is asked whether to take a seat and gives an equivocal answer.
explanation.walkthrough: You sit in a grandstand, but to stand is the opposite of to sit, hence 'yes and no'.
explanation.definitionFit: A grandstand offers seats to spectators, while the verb means to be upright on one's feet.

clue.text: All but the last of the girls turned up in your part of Greece

indicators.note: each of the two words, the and girls, loses its final letter

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned up means read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: lasses are girls
Y is a common abbreviation for your (as in yr)

explanation.surface: Most of the girls arrived in your region of Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All but the last of' trims THE to TH and LASSES to LASSE; 'turned up' makes ESSAL. TH + ESSAL + Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Thessaly is a historic region of central Greece, east of the Pindus mountains.

clue.text: Representation of the 'a' in 'bag' 'gam' or the 'o' in 'pod' forms 3 and 4

definitions.text: Representation of the 'a' in 'bag' 'gam' or the 'o' in 'pod'
definitions.meaning: each quoted word names a group of animals (a gam or pod of whales), and the quoted letter sits at the centre of each
in some British ..., the third and fourth forms (year groups) make up the intermediate stage

explanation.walkthrough: 'gam' and 'pod' are words for a school of whales, so their centre letters are the very centre of a school.
explanation.definitionFit: An intermediate school between primary and secondary, covering the central year groups, fits both readings.

clue.text: Go having bagged silver after entering castle in the Bristol channel

indicators.note: the trapped piece comes after the opening letter, placing that letter at the front
bagging something means taking it inside, so silver goes within the word for go
the entrance to a word is its opening letter, so this takes the first letter of castle

parts.note: to leave is to go
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: A ship sails off, carrying silver, after entering a castle on the Bristol Channel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bristols' is British rhyming slang (Bristol City, titty) for breasts, so the channel between them is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A cleavage is the hollow between a woman's breasts, jokingly a channel between the Bristols.

clue.text: "2000 years minimum in all men undergoing evolution," one's admitted

indicators.note: being admitted means let inside, so one goes into the jumbled letters
evolving means changing form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A scientist declares that all men have been evolving for at least two thousand years.
explanation.walkthrough: 'undergoing evolution' rearranges IN ALL MEN; 'admitted' lets I in. 'Minimum' belongs with '2000 years', since a plural means at least two.
explanation.definitionFit: The plural of a thousand-year span must be two such spans or more, at the very least two thousand years.

clue.text: Form of gambling, items taken randomly from man's beer mug

indicators.note: items picked out at random come in no fixed order, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A lottery where things are pulled at random out of a fellow's beer tankard.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive's S counts here: MANS BEER MUG supplies all eleven letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The numbers game is an illegal lottery in which bettors wager on digits drawn each day.

clue.text: Asian banker's attempt to leave manufacture and trade

indicators.note: the attempt is told to leave, so those letters are taken out

parts.note: industry is manufacturing and commerce collectively
a try is an attempt

explanation.surface: An Asian financier attempts to quit factory work and commerce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banker' is crossword slang for a river, something with banks, not a financier.
explanation.definitionFit: The Indus is a great river flowing through Pakistan, and a river has banks.

clue.text: Sentence #1 from novel email reveals scam from Hell (even words missing!)

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters are formed into a fresh arrangement

parts.note: first of the odd-numbered words kept as fodder
third word, kept as fodder
fifth word, kept as fodder

explanation.surface: An opening line from fiction: an email exposes a fraud from the devil, with gaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'even words missing!' drops 'reveals' and 'from' from 'email reveals scam from Hell', leaving EMAIL SCAM HELL for 'novel' to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the famous opening sentence of Melville's Moby-Dick, the first line of that book.

clue.text: Long side of beef used in first class cut

indicators.note: the pieces are used inside the term for first class

parts.note: A1 (A one) means first-rate
to itch for something is to long for it

indicators.note: the side of a word here means its edge, so take the first letter of beef

explanation.surface: A long flank of beef is put to use in a top-quality cut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long' looks like an adjective for the side of beef but is a verb, and 'first class' must be written out in full as A ONE rather than A1.
explanation.definitionFit: Aitchbone is the rump bone of cattle, and the joint of beef carved over it.

clue.text: A second row about recording, under 5 at a premium

parts.note: B is second in the alphabet, as in plan B

indicators.note: the word for row goes around the other pieces

parts.note: to row is to use an oar, and oar stands for it

indicators.note: in a down clue, something under another comes after it

parts.note: V is the Roman numeral five
an EP is an extended-play record

explanation.surface: A second row at a concert, around a recording, costs a premium.
explanation.walkthrough: '5' is not the cross-reference to 5 Down but the Roman numeral; 'row' is a verb for using an oar.
explanation.definitionFit: Shares above par trade at more than face value, which is selling at a premium.

clue.text: After which, slug it out?

parts.note: having clamped teeth on a slug (a bullet), you might spit it out; the surface suggests a fight

explanation.surface: A challenge: once this is done, settle matters with fists.
explanation.walkthrough: Wounded soldiers once bit a bullet to endure pain; 'slug' is slang for a bullet, so after biting it you could spit the slug out.
explanation.definitionFit: To face up to something unpleasant bravely was once done literally, gripping lead between the teeth.

clue.text: Be inclined endlessly to irritate climber

parts.note: to tend is to be inclined

indicators.note: without its end, so the final letter of the word for irritate goes

parts.note: to rile is to irritate

explanation.surface: Someone tends to annoy a mountaineer without end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'climber' is a plant, not a mountaineer: TEND + RIL(E).
explanation.definitionFit: A tendril is the thin coiling shoot by which a climbing plant grips its support.

clue.text: Shot dead on cross

parts.note: the late king is the dead king
to cut a road is to cross it

explanation.surface: A crack marksman's bullet hits the cross exactly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dead on' reads as 'exactly', but 'on' just joins LATE to CUT. A late cut is a cricket stroke.
explanation.definitionFit: The late cut is a cricket stroke, played by guiding the ball behind the wicket at the last moment.

clue.text: Physicist who's taken on add-on for…

indicators.note: the word on is taken away from the scientist's name

parts.note: Sir Edward Appleton was the British physicist who discovered the ionosphere's reflecting layer
taken as written

explanation.surface: A scientist has signed up as an extra for something continued in the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs into 22, so the add-on is for software from Bill Gates's world.
explanation.definitionFit: An applet is a small program that runs within a larger application such as a browser.

clue.text: Choosy eater, perhaps, with goods in transit?

indicators.note: the goods are loaded inside the vehicle, so 'in' signals a container

parts.note: the Ford Transit is a common British van
e.g. (for example) signals 'perhaps'

explanation.surface: A fussy diner, maybe, with produce on the move.
explanation.walkthrough: 'transit' stands for the Ford Transit, the archetypal British delivery van; 'with goods' only dresses the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: A vegan picks food carefully, eating nothing from animals.

clue.text: … one who made his money from PC World openings

definitions.text: one who made his money from PC World
definitions.meaning: Bill ..., co-founder of Microsoft, grew rich from personal computers
gateways or entrances in a fence or wall

explanation.walkthrough: PC World is a British computer retailer, but here it means the personal-computer world generally.
explanation.definitionFit: The Microsoft founder's surname is also the plural for the hinged barriers that open a fence.

clue.text: Confectioner's relief across street on grass

indicators.note: the street abbreviation stretches across, around, the word for relief

parts.note: a wee gives relief, as in relieving oneself
to shop someone, like to grass, is to inform on them

explanation.surface: Confectioner's relief carving across a street, on a lawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'relief' suggests sculpture but means a wee, relieving oneself; 'grass' and 'shop' are both British slang for informing on someone.
explanation.definitionFit: A confectioner's is a store selling candy, which Britons call a sweetshop.

clue.text: Safe to criticise eternal youth

parts.note: peter is old criminal slang for a safe
to pan a play is to criticise it harshly

explanation.surface: It's safe to knock the idea of staying young for ever.
explanation.walkthrough: A safe-cracker was a peterman in British underworld slang.
explanation.definitionFit: J. M. Barrie's boy who never grew up embodies endless boyhood.

clue.text: See 9
I'll decide about you

parts.note: re means about, as in business letters
you, doing this puzzle, are the solver

explanation.surface: Someone asserts their authority: they'll make the call on you.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer speaks: as one who settles things, it says 'I'll decide'.
explanation.definitionFit: A resolver is one who settles or determines a question, speaking here in the first person.

clue.text: Lying down in big crowd at Lord's? Right to take time out

parts.note: at means in, as in 'at home'

indicators.note: right is to take the place of time, which goes out

parts.note: a Test match draws big crowds at Lord's, the London cricket ground

explanation.surface: Lying down in a big cricket crowd, someone is entitled to a break.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord's is a London cricket ground that hosts Test matches; in TEST, R replaces the first T to give REST.
explanation.definitionFit: To be at rest is to be still and reposing, as when stretched out horizontally.
